title: A sense of scale
summary_es: Divulgación científica: por qué no podemos imaginar lo muy grande, lo muy pequeño ni lo muy antiguo, y por qué haberlo medido es una hazaña.
prediction_prompt: Can you really imagine a light year, or a billion years? What tricks help us to picture such numbers?

sentences.text: There is a peculiar kind of dizziness that comes from thinking seriously about size.
Not the size of mountains or oceans, which we can at least walk towards, but the size of things that lie entirely outside the range of our senses.
Human intuition evolved to cope with objects between, roughly, a grain of sand and a horizon.
Beyond those limits, in either direction, our imagination begins to fail, and we fall back on numbers that we can write down but cannot feel.
Consider distance.
Light, the fastest thing there is, could circle the Earth more than seven times in a single second.
Even so, it takes eight minutes to arrive from the Sun, which means that the Sun you see is always slightly out of date.
Jupiter is some forty minutes away at the same speed, and the outermost planet about four hours.
The light from the next nearest star has been travelling for over four years.
Were that star to vanish tonight, we would go on admiring it, in perfect ignorance, for another four years.
Astronomers have long recognised that statements of this kind, however accurate, tend to slide off the mind.
Their solution has usually been the scale model.
Shrink the Sun to the size of a grapefruit, and the Earth becomes a grain of salt about fifteen metres away.
On the same scale, the nearest star would be another grapefruit, some four thousand kilometres distant.
The most striking feature of such a model is not the objects but the gaps between them.
A model that included the edge of our own galaxy would no longer fit on the planet.
The universe, it turns out, consists overwhelmingly of nothing.
The same disorientation awaits us if we travel inwards rather than outwards.
A single drop of water contains more molecules than there are stars in our galaxy; indeed, more than there are grains of sand on all the beaches of the world.
Each of those molecules is, in turn, mostly empty space.
If the nucleus of an atom were enlarged to the size of a pea and placed in the centre of a football stadium, its electrons would be circling somewhere among the highest seats.
Solid matter, including the table on which this page may be resting, owes its solidity not to being full but to the forces that hold all that emptiness in shape.
Time presents an even stiffer challenge.
The usual device here is to compress the entire history of the Earth into a single year.
On this calendar, the planet forms on the first of January.
Life appears surprisingly early, perhaps in March, yet remains microscopic until late autumn.
The dinosaurs arrive in the middle of December and are gone by the twenty-sixth.
Our own species turns up roughly half an hour before midnight on New Year's Eve.
The whole of recorded history, with its empires, its cathedrals and its arguments, occupies the final half-minute or so.
It would be easy to draw a gloomy conclusion from all this.
Measured against such scales, a human life is an almost invisibly thin slice of an almost invisibly small place, and some writers have found the thought unbearable.
It is, after all, the oldest of human anxieties: that we do not matter.
Yet there is another way of looking at it, and it seems to me the more convincing one.
The remarkable fact is not that we are small.
It is that a creature so small, and so recently arrived, has managed to work any of this out.
Nothing in our evolutionary past required us to know the distance to a star or the age of a rock.
No other animal, as far as we can tell, has ever wondered how old the ground beneath it is.
We discovered these things anyway, using instruments built by hand and reasoning refined over a few dozen generations.
The measurement of the universe is, among other things, a human achievement, and arguably the least likely one of all.
So the dizziness may be worth cultivating rather than avoiding.
It is the feeling of the mind reaching the edge of what it was built for, and then, with some effort, taking one further step.
Few sensations are more characteristic of our species, and none, perhaps, does it greater credit.

language_focus.explanation_es: *The measurement of the universe*, *the same disorientation*, *its solidity*: convertir verbos y adjetivos en nombres condensa la información y da al texto un tono más abstracto y formal.
*Were that star to vanish tonight* = *If that star vanished tonight*. Sin *if* y con el verbo delante: es formal y muy propio del ensayo.

options.text: Schools teach mathematics badly in most countries nowadays
